To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sperm incubated in a medium containing strontium instead of calcium undergo the capacitation process, but do not undergo spontaneous acrosome reaction.
the replacement of calcium (Ca(2+) )for strontium (Sr (2+)) in hamster sperm medium is an excellent tool to separate capacitation and the acrosome response.
the replacement of calcium (Ca(2+) for strontium (Sr2+)) in the incubation media for hamster spermatozoa, allows sperm capacitation and ZP-binding, without undergoing spontaneous acrosome reaction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of replacing Ca(2+) for Sr(2+) during sperm incubation on sperm function.
the use of Sr(2+) instead of Ca(2+) as a tool to analyze capacitation and AR.
the use of Sr(2+) as a substitute for Ca(2+) in the study of the capacitation process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ca(2+) and Sr(2+) are not interchangeable for the AR.
Ca(2+) and Sr(2+) behave differently in sperm incubation medium, and the latter would not be able to replace Ca(2+) in the AR.
Sr(2+) can replace Ca(2+) for sperm capacitation but not for the AR.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the absence of spontaneous AR in Sr2+-sperm is due to an active ENa(+) channel, and that this channel is not active in Ca(2+) -incubated sperm.
Sr(2+) is able to support the early capacitation events, but is not able to induce the AR.
the replacement of Ca(2+) with Sr(2+) allows capacitation and ZP binding, but not AR.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, even though Sr(2+) can substitute for Ca(2+) in some sperm functions, the absence of Na(+)-dependent ENaC activity in Sr(2+) is the main reason why sperm incubated in this ion are unable to undergo spontaneous AR.
Sr(2+) can substitute Ca(2+) as a divalent cation for capacitation but not for AR.
, in contrast to what has been reported for other mammalian species, Sr(2+), at least in hamster, is not an effective Ca(2+) substitute for the AR.
